article_text:
国立科学博物館（東京・上野公園）で特別展「生きものたちの性」が10月31日、開幕しました。科博が初めて“性”をテーマに据えた展覧会の公式アンバサダーは、NHKのEテレで性を考える番組に出演中のお笑いコンビ、ラランド（サーヤ、ニシダ）。音声ガイドを務めた立場も踏まえ、本展の魅力を語ってもらいました。

特別展「生きものたちの性」

会場：国立科学博物館（東京都台東区上野公園7-20）

会期：2026年10月31日（土）～2027年2月21日(日)

開館時間：9時～17時(入場は16時30分まで)

休館日：毎週月曜日、11月4日(水)、11月24日(火)、12月28日(月)～1月1日(金・祝)、1月12日(火) ※ただし、11月2日(月)、23日(月・祝)、1月11日(月・祝)、2月15日(月)は開館

入場料：一般・大学生2,300円（2,100円）、小・中・高校生600円（500円） ※（ ）は前売り料金

アクセス：JR「上野駅」公園口より徒歩5分／東京メトロ銀座線・日比谷線「上野駅」より徒歩10分

詳細は、 展覧会公式サイト または 国立科学博物館公式サイト まで。

公式アンバサダーは夢だった

オープニングイベントに登場した二人。サーヤさんは「小さい頃からよく科博に来ていて、いつか公式アンバサダーをやるのが夢でした」と秘めたる野望を明かしました。「そんな夢、持つ子いますか」とニシダさんが突っ込みます。それでも、「性の展覧会だから、ラランドにはピッタリだと思いました」とサーヤさんが強調すると、ニシダさんも「このテーマでなければ、一生、アンバサダー（の仕事）はなかったと思います」と同意しました。

ーーEテレの教養番組「はなしちゃお！～性と生の学問」があっての仕事ですね。

サーヤ「すごい反響があって、NHKなのに民放でもギリギリのところまで手を出しちゃっています。外国の性教育はずっと進んでいるので、日本とのギャップを埋めることを、説教臭くなくやるようにしています」

ーー音声ガイドはどうでしたか？

ニシダ「掛け合いだったので、普段のラジオのテンションに近くできました。厳かにならないで、くだけた感じで。このテーマにはちょうどいい男女二人コンビなので、女性にとっても男性にとっても聞きやすいと思います」

コモドオオトカゲ式に少子高齢化解決？

ーー印象に残った展示はありましたか？

サーヤ「コモドオオトカゲはひとりで子供を作って産めるそうです。人だったらすごいですよね。少子高齢化も解決するだろうし」

ニシダ「性、子育てとか性別の決定とか、我々が思っている性と角度の違うものもありました。下ネタっぽいものでなく、神秘的なものを感じました」

サーヤ「動物の展示でも人と似たところがあるなと思いました。マッチョ性で売るとか、プレゼントで近づくとか、女の子っぽくして仲良くするとか、『こういう友達いるわ』っていう見方をしても面白い」

ーー来場者には展覧会のどこを見てほしいですか？

サーヤ「キャッチーなものが多かったので、生きもの好きも、そうでない人も誰でもフラットに楽しめる気がします。話のついでに来てもらいたいです。特に親子で来てほしいですね。性の話の前に、動物や植物の展示でワンクッション入ると、スムーズに話ができると思います」

ーー科博には本当に子供の頃から来ていたんですか？

サーヤ「小中学校の自由研究とかで、科学博物館には本当によく来ていました。毎回真剣に見ちゃいます。大学生の頃も安かったのでちょこちょこ来ていましたが、大人料金になったら高くなっちゃった」

ニシダ「アンバサダーなら顔パスで入れるかな。自分が載っているフライヤー持って行こう」

とても周囲に気を配りながら、大役を務めているお二人でした。ちなみに、コモドオオトカゲは卵生ですが、オスがいないときにのみ、メスが「単為生殖」をするそうです。単為生殖で生まれる子はオスのみになるんだとか。必要なオスを自分で産んでしまうわけです。また、国立科学博物館の大学生料金は一般と同額ですが、関東の多くの大学は同館のパートナーシップ校となっていて、常設展無料、特別展割引などの特典があります。（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・丸山謙一）

article_text:
C arol Morley’s self-portrait of the artist as a young woman is rich, tender and terribly funny and sad: a study in the chaos of being young and a triptych of childhood, girlhood and youth, with some daring touches of Terence Davies. It is about the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self, even as the things you thought permanent suddenly collapse – including the background stability of your poor old mum and dad. And it’s also about the untold, unacknowledged story of sadness that lay behind the angry blaze of punk and new wave. Watching this I thought of something I’d assumed lost for ever: my own feelings, aged 17, on hearing Buzzcocks’ Sixteen: “… I wish I was 16 again / Then things would be such fun / All the things I’d do would be the same / But they’re much more fun / Than when you’re 21.” Could it be, I thought, that I’m already sad about not being 16?

7 Miles Out is based on Morley’s autobiographical novel of the same title , the once-upon-a-time-in-Stockport story of Ann, played with charm and zing by Lucy Halliday, and as a sweetly innocent young girl by Amelie Hughes. Young Ann pretends to be making a radio programme with her cassette recorder the way so many did in the 1970s, and hero-worships her would-be rock journalist elder brother Scott (Kasper Hilton-Hille) – based on Morley’s brother Paul – who is already plugged into the burgeoning post-punk and new wave scene.

Ann’s mum Bryn, wonderfully played by Gemma Whelan, is capable and good-humoured in a no-nonsense sort of way, but later to be beset with anger and mercurial depression. She has however found something to smile about now in the news that her husband and Ann’s dad Ronald, played by Aidan Gillen, has found a prestigious new job in Manchester – seven miles out. So to get to work, he has apparently been supplied with a handsome, though not brand-new car.

Ronald exudes a dangerous and almost radioactive aura of angry discontent that Gillen knows how to project. Sitting on his armchair, smoking and watching TV still dressed in suit and slightly loosened tie, Gillen’s Ronald plays along with Ann’s artless requests for a radio interview on the subject of his exciting new professional future. He is capable of romantic gestures and gentleness, which perhaps baffle and unnerve his family. What exactly has got into him? What has he decided upon?

Ronald’s terrible fate is to govern the rest of Ann’s life, even as she gets bullied and then thrown out of school (a place as brutally uncaring as anything in Kes); she later has to live in a grisly boarding house that her mum hates. Ann tries to start a band with her best mate Hel (Leila Entwistle) – perhaps more than best mate – in imitation of her heroes, Joy Division . She yearns for the musical scene in Manchester, to escape her pain, to cauterise the agony of what happened to her dad, and nullify her own wretchedness in never being able to tell anyone. There are three people who take their own lives in this movie, but the only one without a shame-filled cover-up is Ian Curtis, lead singer of Joy Division.

Ann’s attempts to get tickets to see Joy Division, and then to see Joy Division without tickets, are gripping in themselves and bring us to that figure who somehow looms inevitably large in any representation of this subject: TV presenter, Factory Records owner and co-founder of the Haçienda club, Tony Wilson (played here by Jim English); he is one of the many supercilious individuals who let Ann down and won’t let her and her mates in to see the band. Later when Ann descends into depression and drinking, she ringingly denounces the pompous Wilson: “I’ve shagged him; he gave me my first croissant!” It’s a line so surreal that it has to be taken from life.

And so Ann gets further and further into the music scene, closer and closer to a reckoning with her own pain – but then mysteriously goes away from it, or through it or past it. Is it something she has dealt with or simply found a way of burying? There is a tricky encounter with a London music promoter, played in cameo by Claire Grogan; Ann can’t forgive her for something she says about Curtis. This poignant, smart film is such a pleasure.

article_text:
Chanel is deepening its relationship with Hong Kong’s M+ museum , signing on as its lead partner for the next three years and expanding its support beyond film to exhibitions, artist programs, and other projects.

The French luxury house has backed M+, the contemporary visual culture museum in Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District, since 2023. The partnership has until now mostly focused on experimental cinema, film restoration, and building the museum’s moving-image collection. The new agreement, announced Wednesday, will bring Chanel into a much broader range of the museum’s activities.

At the center of the deal is a new initiative called “Pioneering Visions,” which will spotlight artists whose work has helped shape contemporary art and visual culture, particularly those from Hong Kong, mainland China, and across in Asia.

The first exhibition under the program will be Sarah Sze : Centrifuge , a solo presentation opening at the museum’s M+ Focus Gallery in February 2027. The initiative will also include artist talks, screenings, workshops, and an online platform featuring works from the museum’s collection.

Financial terms of the expanded partnership were not disclosed.

For Chanel, the agreement marks another step in its growing involvement with major cultural institutions through the Chanel Culture Fund , which also supports programs at the British Film Institute, Berlin’s Hamburger Bahnhof, and the Venice Biennale.

Yana Peel , Chanel’s president of arts, culture, and heritage, described M+ in a statement as one of the company’s earliest institutional arts partners in Asia and praised the museum’s role in establishing Hong Kong as an international cultural center.

“Now, after successful programmes focused on moving image, we are [broadening] our scope.” She added that “M+ is so much more than a museum: it is the epicenter for dialogue within Asia and between Asia and the world.”

The partnership has already produced some tangible results. Since 2023, Chanel has supported the restoration of nine Hong Kong feature films, which have since been shown at more than 130 screenings around the world. The museum has also acquired 60 experimental moving-image works, roughly half of them from Hong Kong.

Chanel has also supported a senior curatorial position dedicated to moving image and the museum’s Asian Avant-Garde Film Festival, which has attracted more than 10,300 participants across three editions since 2024.

Those efforts will continue under the new agreement. All nine restored films are scheduled to screen at M+ in November, while another six films from across Asia are due to be released through the restoration program in 2027.

M+ director Suhanya Raffel said in a statement the expanded partnership would allow the museum to move beyond its initial emphasis on cinema and explore connections between different artistic disciplines.

The announcement comes as M+, which opened in 2021, approaches its fifth anniversary. Designed by Herzog & de Meuron, the waterfront museum houses more than 9,000 works spanning contemporary art, design, architecture, and moving image, including the M+ Sigg Collection of Chinese contemporary art.

article_text:
Die kürzlich auf Deutsch erschienene Graphic Novel „Der Leib Christi“ kreist um eine Mutter-Tochter-Geschichte im Schatten einer psychischen Erkrankung und religiöser Wahnvorstellungen. Das Besondere des autobiografisch inspirierten Werks der spanischen Künstlerin Bea Lema ist seine auf Textilarbeiten bauende Ästhetik, die Lema jüngst auch bei der Adaption des Stoffes für einen Kurzfilm aufgegriffen hat.

In diesem Jahr sorgte ein animierter Kurzfilm der Spanierin Bea Lema bei Festivals für Aufsehen: „ El cuerpo del Cristo “, zu Deutsch „Der Leib Christi“. Die größte Besonderheit des kleinen Werks ist ein außergewöhnliches Stilmittel, nämlich abgefilmte Bilder aus Stoff und Stickerei. Ein herrlich haptisch anmutendes Werk, das 2026 mit dem „Silbernen Drachen“ für die beste Regie in der Kurzfilmkonkurrenz des Filmfestivals in Krakau geehrt wurde. Die kleine Arbeit stellt das Regiedebüt der 1985 geborenen Künstlerin dar und ist eine Adaption ihrer gleichnamigen Graphic Novel, die 2017 in Lemas Heimat Spanien erschien, ihr diverse Preise einbrachte und die nun seit Oktober 2026 beim Verlag Reprodukt auch in einer deutschen Auflage erschienen ist.

Auch der Comic-Look basiert auf Stoff und Stickerei

Der Look des Kurzfilms ist im Comic „ Der Leib Christi “ schon angelegt. Auch hier bilden Stoff und Stickerei die Basis, ergänzt durch Zeichnungen, die sich dem Stil der Textilarbeiten anschmiegen. Ähnlich wie der Inhalt ist auch die Technik autobiografisch beeinflusst. Die Arbeit mit Stoff und Garn verbindet Bea Lema mit ihrer Mutter, die als Schneiderin gearbeitet hat. Sie dient als Medium der Geschichte einer Mutter-Tochter-Beziehung, die von einer schweren psychischen Erkrankung der Mutter überschattet ist, sowie den Belastungen, die daraus für die Familie und insbesondere für die Tochter erwachsen.

Die spanische Religiosität und der Volksglaube spielen darin eine nicht unwichtige Rolle. Die psychische Störung der Mutter manifestiert sich, befeuert vom tiefreligiösen ländlichen Umfeld, in Wahnvorstellungen von teuflischen Heimsuchungen und in Ängsten vor dem „bösen Blick“ mutmaßlich feindlich gesinnter Nachbarn. Die Versuche, dem Leiden mit Hilfe religiöser bis abergläubischer Praktiken wie Wallfahrten oder dem Besuch einer „Meiga“, einer „weißen Hexe“, Herr zu werden, bleiben unwirksam. Aber auch die auf Psychopharmaka setzende nervenärztliche Betreuung erweist sich als unzureichend; sie versagt nicht zuletzt dabei, die Angehörigen zu beraten und zu unterstützen.

Ein Passionsweg aus Angst und Liebe

Die Konsequenzen für die Tochter sind drastisch, da die Sorge um die Mutter das Heranwachsen des Mädchens überschattet. Ein Passionsweg aus Angst und Liebe, den Lema in eindrückliche Bilder fasst. Deren Farbigkeit und Luftigkeit – Pastelltöne und leicht anmutende Striche, Punkte und Stiche auf heller Fläche – scheinen die Schwere des Inhalts konterkarieren zu wollen, sind vor allem aber ein großartiges Ausdrucksmittel, um den Figuren etwas ungemein Zart-Fragiles zu geben, das die Geschichte umso anrührender macht. Mit Schwarz arbeitet Lema fast nur, um die Teufels-Fantasien umzusetzen. Und es kommt in einer besonders schmerzhaften Passage zum Einsatz, in der sich in schwarzem Faden auf weißem Stoff Rückblicke in Kindheit und Jugend der Mutter im Schatten eines gewalttätigen, alkoholsüchtigen Vaters entfalten.

Visuell faszinierend

„Der Leib Christi“ entfaltet eine ebenso suggestive wie visuell faszinierende Autofiktion um transgenerational sich fortschreibende Traumata, um Wahn, Psychiatrie und Glauben. Die deutsche Veröffentlichung der Comic-Novel erlaubt es auch hierzulande, Bea Lema als Autorin wahrzunehmen. Auf ihren Kurzfilm und künftige Projekte muss man hingegen noch warten.

article_text:
El thriller dirigido por Scott Waugh combina persecuciones, humor y una historia de redención que encuentra en sus protagonistas su mayor fortaleza. Aunque tiene algunos problemas para equilibrar sus distintos tonos, ofrece una aventura de acción entretenida.

Hay películas que no necesitan reinventar un género para entretener. “ Entrega al límite ” ( Runner ) recupera la fórmula clásica del cine de acción: una misión contrarreloj, sicarios dispuestos a todo y dos protagonistas de personalidades totalmente opuestas que deberán trabajar juntos. Con Alan Ritchson y Owen Wilson al frente, la película encuentra en la dupla el principal atractivo.

¿De qué va la cinta?

La historia sigue a Hank Malone (Ritchson), un exintegrante de los Navy SEAL que trabaja como una especie de mensajero en Australia mientras intenta reconstruir su vida tras una tragedia personal y un pasado marcado por el alcoholismo. Su día cambia drásticamente cuando recibe el encargo de transportar un hígado destinado a una niña que necesita un trasplante urgente. El problema es que deberá completar la entrega acompañado por Ben Bishop (Wilson), un mensajero especializado que no puede separarse del órgano y que resulta mucho más hablador que su nuevo compañero.

La misión se complica cuando una organización criminal intenta quedarse con el hígado, cuyo valor en el mercado ilegal es extraordinario por su compatibilidad con un grupo sanguíneo poco frecuente. Liderados por Damian Zaldívar (Rodrigo Santoro), los sicarios convierten el traslado en una persecución en la que realmente cada minuto cuenta.

La dupla es lo que sostiene la película

Ritchson, sin dudas, impone su presencia física y sus condiciones para el cine de acción, en un papel que rememora al mejor “Reacher”. Sin embargo, su Hank no es solamente un hombre capaz de derrotar a varios adversarios: también debe controlar sus impulsos, superar sus pérdidas y mantenerse alejado de la violencia (cómo dice al principio del film).

Wilson funciona como su contraposición. Con su habitual estilo descontracturado, digno de él, interpreta a un hombre que nunca deja de hablar y no está preparado para enfrentarse a un Cartel. Sus chisten alivianan la tensión y genera algunos intercambios divertidos con Hank, aunque l a película podría haber aprovechado mejor la química entre ambos .

Te puede interesar

La relación entre Hank y Ben también permite introducir una idea que atraviesa la historia: la posibilidad de aprender de alguien completamente diferente . Mientras uno debe encontrar motivos para volver a involucrarse con los demás, el otro descubre que no todo se resuelve hablando. La dupla funciona, aunque no siempre alcanza el potencial que promete.

Acción efectiva, pero con algunos excesos

En las cámaras, Scott Waugh aprovecha su experiencia en el cine de acción como Proyecto extracción y Los Indestructibles 4 , para construir persecuciones automovilísticas de alto vuelo y peleas que mantienen el ritmo. Las secuencias físicas son uno de los puntos fuertes de la película, especialmente cuando Ritchson despliega sus habilidades frente a adversarios que parecen no darle respiro. Huesos rotos, heridas de cuchillos, balas y sangre, hay por doquier.

Es justamente, la acumulación de violencia la que termina siendo excesiva por momentos y contrasta con el humor y el costado emotivo del relato . La película salta entre el thriller, la comedia de compañeros y el drama personal sin conseguir siempre que esas piezas se entrelazen en el desarrollo. Algunos personajes secundarios, incluido el villano interpretado por Santoro y Leila George que se pone en la piel de Kate Baker, podrían haber tenido un desarrollo más sólido.

La lucha de Hank por mantenerse sobrio y dejar atrás un pasado doloroso acompaña una misión en la que la vida de una niña depende de sus decisiones. Esa dimensión emocional le da un propósito al protagonista, aunque no todas las situaciones consiguen transmitir la misma fuerza.

Una propuesta entretenida

“Entrega al límite” no reinventa el cine de acción, pero sabe como hacer que sus protagonistas ofrezcan una aventura dinámica. Ritchson aporta contundencia y un costado vulnerable, mientras Wilson suma humor y ligereza a una historia que, sin él, correría el riesgo de tomarse demasiado en serio .

Con algunos problemas de tono y una violencia que a veces le resta impacto a sus propias escenas, la película encuentra sus mejores momentos en la relación entre sus protagonistas y en la búsqueda de redención de Hank. Una propuesta recomendable para quienes disfrutan de las películas de acción clásicas, con una dupla que demuestra que la fortaleza no siempre se mide por la cantidad de golpes que uno puede dar.

Post cinta, se puede comparar a la misma con Un espía y medio de Dwayne Johnson («La Roca») y Kevin Hart ; o con varias de Jason Statham debido a las escenas de acción exageradas.

Calificación: 5.5/10.

article_text:
Andrew Garfield is set to receive the Maltin Modern Master Award at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival on Feb. 6.

Joining film critic Leonard Maltin for an on-stage conversation, Garfield will reflect on his decades-long career, including his upcoming performance in Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” where he plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

“Andrew Garfield has long since proven himself to critics and audiences alike,” Maltin said. “It’s no simple matter to balance a career between mainstream Hollywood movies and challenging director-driven projects, but he has done exactly that and done it well.”

Throughout his career, Garfield has received two Academy Award nominations and won a Golden Globe and Tony Award. His credits include Mel Gibson’s “Hacksaw Ridge,” David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” Martin Scorsese’s “Silence” and Luca Guadagnino’s “After The Hunt.” He also starred as Peter Parker in “The Amazing Spider-Man” films and earned an Emmy nomination for “Under the Banner of Heaven.”

The Modern Master Award was established in 1995 to celebrate an individual who enriched culture through their work in film. It was later renamed the Maltin Modern Master Award in 2015 in honor of film critic and long-time SBIFF moderator Leonard Maltin.

Garfield joins a lineup of past recipients that includes Adam Sandler, Angelina Jolie, Jamie Lee Curtis, Nicole Kidman, Javier Bardem, Robert Downey Jr., Denzel Washington, Cate Blanchett, George Clooney, Christopher Plummer, Christopher Nolan, James Cameron, Sean Penn, Clint Eastwood and Peter Jackson.

The 42nd SBIFF will take place Feb. 3-13 and will feature screenings, filmmaker Q&As, industry panels and celebrity tributes.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: UK agency Independent Creative Management (ICM) has signed Havoc actor Serhat Metin .

Metin is known for last year playing a detective, Cortez, in Netflix’s Havoc , the police action thriller starring Tom Hardy, Timothy Oliphant, Forest Whitaker and Jessie Mei Li.

He has also appeared in Havoc director Gareth Evans’s Sky series Gangs of London , and has credits for Michael Flatley’s Blackbird , Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen in 2019 and the likes of Aladin , The Mummy , American Assassin and Patient Zero .

Related Stories

Tom Prior Signs With Independent Creative Management

Tracee Ellis Ross, Lake Bell & Ken Leung Thriller 'Blow The Horn' Heads To AFM For Sales

The Turkish-Cypriot actor is based in London and began his acting career after transitioning from amateur boxing in 2011.

Watch on Deadline

He joins the likes of Tom Prior, Shane Afolabi, Nathaniel Jacobs, Eshe Asante and Erol Ismail on the books at ICM, which is part of Independent Creative Group and led by CEO Katerina Michael.

“I’m delighted to have joined ICM and have been incredibly pleased with the support and opportunities they’ve provided in such a short space of time,” said Metin.

“Katerina and the team at ICM understand my vision for my acting career and we are definitely on the same page regarding the next steps. I’m excited to be working with a team that understands my vision and shares my enthusiasm for what lies ahead.”

Michael said ICM would “look forward to supporting him as he takes the next exciting step in his career,” and added: “I’m extremely confident that Serhat has a very promising future ahead of him. He has a fantastic presence, genuine talent and all the qualities needed to build a successful career.”

article_text:
Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends honours the pioneers, icons and activists who have inspired the photographer on his life journey

Entering Tim Walker’s F airyland is, as the title suggests, like entering another world. The stark minimalism of the white-cube gallery is banished, the established formality of the National Portrait Gallery fades away. Instead the opening room is painted bold lavender and a giant hand reaches out from one wall, holding aloft a flower. The introductory wall text includes squiggly doodles and illustrations, and is written in the first person; there is a sweet family photograph, showing the artist as a young boy, proudly sporting fairy wings. “It’s a picture of Tim from 1975, taken by his mum Lorna,” smiles Susanna Brown, curator of Fairyland . “When Tim showed it to me last year I said, ‘We need to open the exhibition with that because it sets the scene for the whole project’.”

In his introduction, Walker writes he was “born happily gay” on 27 November 1970. Creative, imaginative, nurtured by his supportive mother; he soon learned that “society said my nature was wrong” and invented Fairyland as an escape, “a place where I would go to be myself, dreaming up romances and adventures”. Later, the word ‘fairy’ also became tainted, used as a homophobic taunt by his peers; growing up and watching news of HIV and AIDS’ spread – including the UK’s grim public health campaign on it – Walker started to feel that being Queer was dangerous, even shameful. It is only now, in his fifties, that he feels able to publicly embrace his sexuality with this exhibition, which he has been working on for six years. Subtitled Love and Legends , it includes portraits of Queer icons and fellow-travellers who have inspired Walker over the years; the selection of sitters is firmly subjective, a personal take on those who have helped build the world he now lives within.

“I have the chance to tell the next generations that you are not alone. Your difference is your power. Difference is a precious and beautiful thing” – Tim Walker

“It’s not a who’s who of all the brilliant Queer people today,” says Brown. “That would be an impossibly huge exhibition! It’s about Tim and his journey, both as a photographer and a creative, and the progress of his work.” Brown has known Walker for over a decade, and has previously worked with him on the exhibition Tim Walker: Wonderful Things at the V&A in 2019-20 ; the exhibition design is by Shona Heath, who has collaborated with Walker for 30 years. Flamboyant colour tracks through the exhibition, with rooms painted in rainbow hues from bright red and yellow to more sombre black and dark green. It is joyful but there is a serious edge, the first half of the show honouring and acknowledging the activists who fought for the right to love, and the hard years of the AIDS crisis.

In fact Fairyland looks back to these early years. In 2020 Walker stumbled on a plaque in London’s Highbury Fields commemorating the UK’s first public gay rights protest and realised he was born on the same day. The effort to create the world in which Walker now flourishes had been going on his whole life, and this discovery sparked his curiosity about those civil rights pioneers, and he set out on an odyssey to photograph them. This show stems from that impulse, and the fact it is taking place in the NPG is important, because the NPG is a national institution dedicated to celebrating individuals’ contributions to the UK. Walker’s exhibition reads as intervention, questioning who gets to be honoured, and why.

Walker plays with this setting in his portraits; in the first room of photographs he references oil paintings in the NPG’s collection dating back to the 1500s. “Holbein and Hilliard memorialised the movers and shakers of the Tudor aristocracy for hundreds of years to come,” he writes in his introduction. “The trailblazers I photographed made history and deserve to be on our gallery walls too.” The first room in Fairyland features Shân Veillard-Thomas and Lisa Power, among others, early activists with the Gay Liberation Front and Stonewall; they are photographed in the style of these paintings, and also framed the same way, the NPG gamely embracing the effort to ‘queer’ its space. “The NPG very kindly allowed us to use some of its beautiful historical frames,” says Brown. “Several of the ornate frames we used [in the show] are hundreds of years old, and then Tim included antique frames within the photographic compositions, so we end up with stunning trompe l’oeil effects.”

All the portraits in Fairyland are creative collaborations between Walker and the sitter, as Brown points out. Gay actress and activist Liz Carr, for example, explained to him that when she was growing up her teachers often cast her as the monarch in school plays due to her wheelchair, lazily reasoning she was already sitting in a kind of throne. Carr and Walker collaborated on an image depicting her as Queen Elizabeth as in the famous ‘Ditchley Portrait’ held by the NPG and dating back to around 1592; the image allows Carr to reclaim her queenliness on her own terms, and it also comes with a twist. “Every single thing in the picture is made of paper – her dress, her shoes, her earrings, the little dog, all of the walls, the ceiling, it’s all wallpaper,” says Brown. “As Liz explains in the audioguide, the paper is a metaphor. When people look at Liz, a Queer disabled woman, they might make certain assumptions, but we know that those assumptions and biases are paper thin. Liz has the power to scrunch up every bit of paper and tear down every wrong assumption, and be exactly who she is.”

Walker sometimes suggested ideas to his sitters, but remained open to their wishes on how to represent themselves. He and Brown have also welcomed sitters’ own voices into the exhibition, by including many quotes in the biographical image labels and 15 different sitters’ voices on the free audio guides, rather than the more conventional artist-curator dialogue. “It was more work to do it that way but I’m glad we did,” says Brown. “It adds a beautiful layer to the exhibition. We’re not only showing people’s faces, we’re also bringing their voices into this building.”

This sense of dialogue runs through the exhibition. The project grew organically, says Brown, sitters recommending friends who Walker could photograph, the portraits therefore representing an interconnected web of people. Queer people in the UK faced – and still face – discrimination, but Fairyland testifies to their ability to create community. Another important strand in the exhibition is intersectionality, because many of the individuals depicted were also fighting off other discriminations – Carr fending off ableism, for example, and Sunil Gupta and Aariana Rose Philip campaigning against racism. As Walker puts it in his introduction; “I have the chance to tell the next generations that you are not alone. Your difference is your power. Difference is a precious and beautiful thing.”

Gupta, who helped found Autograph, the association for Black photographers, is represented in a rakish portrait, in which he holds his camera; he has been living with HIV since 1995, so his portrait acts as a bridge – or further connection – between the one room of the exhibition and the next, which gathers stories connected to the early HIV and AIDS crisis in Britain. The NPG space has a slightly tricky layout, says Brown, with one gallery acting as a central corridor with interconnected galleries leading off it, so she carefully considered where to present these images. Including portraits of individuals who survived the crisis and those who cared for them, as well as shots of high-profile campaigners such as singer Jimmy Somerville, this room may evoke difficult memories for visitors. Brown wanted to wanted to honour them with a space that felt like a refuge and a peaceful sanctuary, slightly removed from the busy central flow of the exhibition.

“For me, as a curator, it was so important to make space for people to express their emotions,” says Brown. “Often we go to galleries and museums and feel we have to behave in a very particular sort of way. There’s also a fear around other people’s judgement when we get emotional in public. But here in Fairyland , I hope visitors feel it’s safe to shed some tears as they recall the AIDS crisis, and that it’s also a place where we can remember those we lost and celebrate their lives with joy. We thought a lot about where to place these portraits and knew we wanted the room to feel peaceful and very special, a quiet reflective space. Designer Shona Heath created exactly that atmosphere.”

In the second half of the show the focus moves to the present; the room titled Queer Today features contemporary artists, writers, designers, and other creatives, depicted in sleek contemporary style which contrasts with the Holbein-inspired approach. Walker is a consummate photographer, says Brown, able to master any technique; this section includes artist Jesse Glazzard, pictured carrying a live falcon. Another room is devoted to an ambitious photoshoot with the Rebel Dykes, and is painted dramatic black. The Rebel Dykes forged their community through the Greenham Common protests and ran the lesbian club Chain Reaction in Vauxhall, which included leather nights and performances with motorbikes. Walker drew on Karlheinz Weinberger’s photograph of a 1960s biker girl, and on rockabilly iconography such as leather jackets, motorbikes, and batwing eyeliner, to emphasise the Rebel Dykes’ strength, power and sex-positivity. “I felt they needed a whole room for their big personalities and their big hair,” smiles Brown. “We wanted to make these massive prints.”

Towards the end of Fairyland is a room gathering Pinups , portraits of famous individuals from Elton John and Chappell Roan to Björk and Kate Bush. Not all identify as gay but they are allies and icons to Walker, and to many others; again, the emphasis is on community, connection, freedom and subjectivity, not ghettos or strict categories. The last room is daring, particularly in a gallery such as the NPG, which welcomes many families and school groups; a celebration of sexuality, including it felt essential to both Walker and Brown. Brown points out that Fairyland celebrates the right to express love so it has to include physical as well as emotional forms. This final room is carpeted and the furniture is covered in tactile velvet brocade fabric, lending it a hushed, boudoirish feel; the images draw on art history, from Aubrey Beardsley’s erotic illustrations and Japanese Shunga woodblocks, to exuberant French painter Fragonard and figures from much older mythologies.

Same-sex relationships have a very long history, Walker reminds me, and contemporary affairs take place within a much wider context. “Queerness is as old as humanity, and these images are so joyful,” says Brown. “It’s an ecstatic finale to the show.”

Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends is on show at the National Portrait Gallery , London, until 07 February 2027.

東京都内の美術館やギャラリーを無料のシャトルバスで結び、東京のアートシーンを国内外に発信するアートイベントとして定着してきた「アートウィーク東京（AWT）」では、今年のトークプログラム「AWT TALKS」として、11月5日に東京都現代美術館でディレクターズ・カンバセーション、11月6日に慶應義塾大学三田キャンパスでシンポジウムを開催する。いずれも参加は無料（事前申込制）。 ディレクターズ・カンバセーション「新たなる希望──次世代の美術館を想像する」では、1929年のニューヨーク近代美術館の設立からほぼ1世紀を経て世界各地に広がった近現代美術館のモデルが、経済的な不確実性や技術の急激な変化、社会の分断、人口構成の変化、歴史の語り方をめぐる考え方の変化といった新たな課題に直面するなか、次世代の近現代美術館の姿を考える。登壇者は、ウォーカー・アート・センター（ミネアポリス）のエグゼクティブディレクター、 メアリー・セルティ 、2021年に開館したM+（香港）で同館の建設とコンセプト形成に深く関わってきた芸術監督兼チーフキュレーターの ドリアン・チョン 、ハウス・デア・クンスト（ミュンヘン）で領域横断的なプログラムを展開する芸術監督の アンドレア・リッソーニ 。モデレーターは東京都現代美術館事業企画課長の 飯田志保子 が務める。新しい世代の来館者やコミュニティとの関係づくり、次世代のアートの担い手の育成、美術館が次の100年以降も発展していくための組織・運営の革新という三つの問いを軸に、近現代美術館の優れた実践にすでに備わっている実験精神や想像力、現在形づくられつつある新たな実践に目を向ける。

シンポジウム「不安の記憶──現代美術と歴史の残響」では、歴史そのものがかつてなく激しい論争の対象となり、検閲や抗議、企画の中止、記念碑の撤去・建立・改変などを通じて美術界もその渦中にある現状を出発点に、現代美術が持つ「記憶をつくる力」をいかに編み直すことができるかを問う。登壇者は、展覧会「 望月桂 自由を扶くひと 」（2025–2026）を中心メンバーとして企画した美術史・社会史研究者で望月桂調査団代表の 足立元 、1978年の「パレスチナのための国際美術展」をめぐるアーカイブ展「Past Disquiet」（2015–2025）を共同企画し、故コヨ・クオが芸術監督を務めた第61回ヴェネツィア・ビエンナーレでキュラトリアルアドバイザーを務める ラシャ・サルティ 、20世紀における黒人急進思想とアジアの革命政治との国境を越えたつながりを再検討する展覧会「The Great Camouflage」（2025–2026）を共同企画し、今年のAWTでは映像上映プログラム「AWT VIDEO」のキュレーションを手掛ける X・ジュー＝ノウェル （ロックバンド美術館エグゼクティブディレクター兼チーフキュレーター）。モデレーターは、AWTエディトリアルディレクターの アンドリュー・マークル が務める。本シンポジウムは、アンドリュー・マークルと塩見有子（NPO法人アーツイニシアティヴトウキョウ理事長）の企画により、慶應義塾大学アート・センター、慶應義塾ミュージアム・コモンズと共同で開催する。

昨年のAWT TALKSのシンポジウム「 WHAT’S GOING ON（愛のゆくえ）──アートはいかにして現実をとらえるか 」では、グッゲンハイム美術館副館長兼チーフキュレーターで、2027年開催の ドクメンタ16 のアーティスティックディレクターを務めるナオミ・ベックウィズ、ドクメンタ14のアーティスティックディレクターを務め、昨年のAWT FOCUSを監修したアダム・シムジック、東京都現代美術館学芸員で昨年のAWT VIDEOを監修した岡村恵子の3名がそれぞれ講演を行ない、その後ディスカッションを行なった。また、初の試みとなったディレクターズ・カンバセーション「 21世紀の美術館のあり方 」では、M+芸術監督兼チーフキュレーターのドリアン・チョンをモデレーターに、ノルトライン＝ヴェストファーレン州立美術館館長のスザンヌ・ゲンスハイマー、ソフィア王妃芸術センター館長のマヌエル・セガデ、UCCA現代美術センター館長兼最高経営責任者のフィリップ・ティナリが、美術館の現在と未来をめぐって議論した（いずれのトークもAWTの 公式YouTubeチャンネル で視聴可能）。AWT TALKSではこのほか、オンライントーク、ラウンドテーブル、コレクターを目指す人に向けたガイドツアーやセミナー、未就学児や学生を対象としたアート教育プログラムなど、初心者からアート通まで幅広い層を対象としたプログラムを展開している。 AWTは、東京都内の数多くの美術館やギャラリーが参加し、文化庁の特別協力の下、世界有数のアートフェア、アートバーゼルと提携し、東京における現代美術の創造性と多様性を国内外に発信するアートイベントとして、コロナ禍の2021年のプレ開催を経て2022年より年に一度開催している。本格開催から5回目となる今年は、過去最多となる56の美術館・ギャラリーが参加。2023年に「買える展覧会」として始まった「AWT FOCUS」は、ウィーンのギャラリーフェスティバル「curated by」とのコラボレーションのもと、10会場で10の展覧会を開催する。会期は11月4日から8日までの5日間。

article_text:
Keanu Reeves is in talks to team with James Wan for the filmmaker’s latest project, “The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil” at Paramount Pictures.

The Paramount Pictures movie reimagines the 2019 Korean action-crime thriller starring Don Lee (also known as Ma Dong-seok), who is attached to reprise his role opposite Reeves. The original film — which follows a police officer and a gangster as they reluctantly join forces to track down a serial killer — debuted to rave reviews at the Cannes Film Festival that year.

Wan will direct the film, his first feature since 2023’s “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom.” He will also produce the project alongside Michael Clear and Jason Blum (via Blumhouse Atomic Monster), Lee (Big Punch Global), Sylvester Stallone and D. Matt Geller (Balboa Productions), and Chris S. Lee (B&C Group. Lorenzo di Bonaventura has also come on board to produce. The project has been in the works since 2019, with Wan boarding the production this spring.

Eric Pearson wrote the latest script, based on previous drafts by Shay Hatten and Brian Helgeland. Helgeland and Billy Acumen will executive produce the project.

Reeves is an action movie icon, headlining numerous franchises from “The Matrix” movies to the “John Wick” films. He last starred in AppleTV’s dramedy “Outcome,” directed by Jonah Hill, and voiced Duke Caboom in “Toy Story 5.” He will next reprise his voice role as fan-favorite character Shadow in “Sonic the Hedgehog 4,” which Paramount has dated for March 19, 2027. Reeves is repped by WME and Ziffren Brittenham.

The Hollywood Reporter first reported the actor’s involvement.

article_text:
(Updated with more details) Years in the making, the L.A. courtroom showdown between Rebel Wilson and The Deb producers is not going to trial as scheduled.

In a filing Wednesday that has been agreed upon by all the principals, Wilson’s lead lawyer Allyson K. Thompson asked for the long-set January 19, 2027 trial to be pushed back more than two months. In fact, the Hart Kienle Pentecost attorney also requested to Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Thomas Long that summary judgment hearings currently scheduled for December also be pushed back.

Related Stories

‘The Deb’ Star Charlotte MacInnes Attacks Rebel Wilson In Appeal Against Court Defeat

How Rebel Wilson’s Directorial Debut ‘The Deb’ Descended Into Legal Chaos, Devastating Cast & Crew

A hearing in downtown L.A. is on the books for Friday to address the requests. Still up against some punishing deadlines for depositions and discovery, the parties are aiming to have the trial moved to March 22 next year.

Out of what has been an extremely contentious battle even by Hollywood standards between producers Amanda Ghost , Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden and Deb director Wilson over allegations of misconduct on the film, this latest twist has a much more personal origin.

Watch on Deadline

“Counsel for Ms. Wilson, Ms. Allyson Thompson, was recently diagnosed with breast cancer,” the 24-page ex parte application filing states.

“Ms. Thompon (sic) has been placed on a medical leave for surgery from November 30, 2026, through January 4, 2027, and is currently working reduced hours due to side effects of the disease,” it continues. “The doctor’s note was shared with all counsel for purposes of meeting and conferring. Ms. Thompson would prefer not to have to attach the doctor’s note to the moving papers but will provide the Court with a copy should it require review.”

The document goes on to say: “After notifying all counsel of the issue, the parties held a scheduled telephonic meet and confer on Friday, October 16, 2026, to address this and other discovery matters. During the call, the parties agreed in principle to continue the trial to March 22, 2027, or a later date mutually acceptable to the parties and the Court. They also agreed that the expert-discovery deadlines could be continued with the trial date.”

Even with the usually packed LASC calendar, it is almost a certainty the judge will sign off on the request.

The October 21 filing and the public announcement of Thompson’s heath issues come as Wilson scored successful reviews ( read Deadline’s Glenn Garner’s here ) last month at the Toronto Film Festival for her latest big-screen effort Girl Group . Unlike the TIFF 2024 debut of The Deb , there were no legal dark clouds hanging over that Randall Park and Jennifer Coolidge co-starrer. On the other side of the Pacific, Deb actress Charlotte MacInnes’ appeal of an Australian court’s decision earlier this year that Wilson did not defame her in a series of social media posts continues.

In a separate case Down Under where Wilson countersued the Deb producers, a judge handed the actress a win, of sorts. While Justice Elisabeth Peden determined Wilson had been involved in the creation of a website to attack the producers, she also said Ghost and the other two hadn’t offered any proof it actually hurt their business. To that, AI Film were ordered to pay Wilson’s legal costs of $251,000 and Wilson was ordered to pay the production company under $10.

To that, Rebel Wilson took to social media to celebrate.

“Defending myself has come at an enormous personal, emotional and financial cost,” she wrote, “But I’m proud that I stood my ground—for myself and for others I was trying to protect.”

View this post on Instagram

Still, buried in the finger-pointing, hyperboles and connections to the Blake Lively vs. Justin Baldoni It Ends With Us saga with ongoing claims of dark-arts PR moves and smear sites , The Deb sunk from view pretty swiftly after it was released by Sunrise Films in late August.

According to the American Cancer Society, 1 in 8 American women will have “invasive breast cancer.” Approximately 320,000 cases are anticipated to be identified in 2026. While breast cancer is the second most common form of death from cancer after lung cancer, the ACS also notes “breast cancer death rates have been decreasing steadily since 1989, for an overall decline of 44% through 2023.” They add: “This is most likely the result of finding breast cancer earlier through screening and increased awareness, as well as better treatments.”

Filme tem estreia prevista para 12 de março nos cinemas.

A Universal Pictures divulgou o trailer de “ O Exorcista: Mártires “, novo filme de Mike Flanagan estrelado por Scarlett Johansson . Assista acima à versão legendada e, abaixo, à dublada.

Em “O Exorcista: Mártires”, a detetive Julie Miller (Johansson) põe fim à onda de assassinatos do satânico Padre Sunday (John Leguizamo), mas acaba sendo arrastada de volta à escuridão por um novo serial killer 13 anos depois, quando seu nome aparece escrito com o sangue de um coroinha assassinado nas paredes da cripta de uma igreja.

Além de Johansson e Leguizamo, o elenco conta ainda com Rahul Kohli, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Laurence Fishburne, Sasha Calle, Diane Lane e Jacobi Jupe. Direção e roteiro são de Mike Flanagan.

“O Exorcista: Mártires” tem estreia prevista para 12 de março nos cinemas.

article_text:
After buying Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment in 2022 and Peter Chernin’s North Road earlier this year, Mediawan has enlisted another major Hollywood player, Reese Witherspoon ‘s Hello Sunshine .

As with its previous acquisitions which were financed partly through stock, Mediawan is bringing Witherspoon into its shareholder base, joining a stellar roster of talent and producers who have invested in the Paris-based group, including Pitt, Chernin and Plan B partners Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner, as well as See-Saw’s Iain Canning and Emilie Sherman. The company also launched LuckyChap International, the London-based arm of Margot Robbie’s company, last November.

“For our 10th anniversary today, we’re working with Brad Pitt, Margot Robbie and Reese Witherspoon — all three of whom are extremely creative and recognized as such — it defines the company’s DNA in terms of its independence, its commitment to talent and its creativity,” said Mediawan co-founder and chairman Pierre-Antoine Capton in an exclusive interview with Variety less than a day after unveiling the deal.

Mediawan also managed to pick up Hello Sunshine at a fraction of the $900 million valuation the company had when Blackstone-backed Candle Media acquired a majority stake in 2021.

Variety understands that Mediawan paid on the lower end of tens of millions of dollars, although Capton declined to disclose the exact figure or financial terms.

“I won’t confirm. The bottom line is that we acquired 100% of Hello Sunshine along with Reese and Mediawan, from Candle Media, and the money we’re investing is going toward development and content creation. It’s truly being invested in the company,” said Capton, who credited Chernin and Jesse Jacobs, former shareholders in Hello Sunshine, for bringing the opportunity to Mediawan.

The momentum has shifted in favor of European companies, as traditional Hollywood power players are under pressure to cut costs, streaming platforms are becoming pickier and U.S. indie producers are eager to work in Europe, where they can produce at lower costs and own IP. While Mediawan has made a name for itself in Hollywood in the last five years, another European giant with French roots, Banijay, which just merged with British powerhouse All3Media, is also looking to invest in the U.S. scripted market where it hasn’t yet broken through.

The acquisition of Hello Sunshine by Mediawan also illustrates how much the business has changed since the streaming boom that fueled Hello Sunshine’s previous valuation. Candle Media, founded by former Disney executives Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs, had bet heavily on Witherspoon’s star power, social media presence and book club, but that model became more difficult to monetize in recent years.

On whether Hello Sunshine will fare better under Mediawan than it did under Candle, Capton pointed to the prestigious track record of Witherspoon’s company, notably “Big Little Lies,” “The Morning Show” and the Apple TV series “Lucky,” adapted from a Reese’s Book Club selection.

“They’ve really excelled creatively. That said, unfortunately, from time to time, there are investment deals with companies that may be perceived as financial strategies. That’s not the case for us,” said Capton, who worked on the deal alongside Mediawan CCO Elisabeth D’Arvieu and Guillaume Izabel, head of strategy and M&A. “With Reese, we’re really looking for creativity, independence and vision. That’s what interests us, so we don’t put financial pressure on it. It’s truly an editorial, artistic and creative addition that we’re seeking.”

Capton also said Mediawan intends to bring Reese’s Book Club internationally, including through potential productions in France and elsewhere in Europe.

“For all Mediawan producers — whether they’re Italian, German, British or Australian — access to all the IP that Reese can leverage through her book club is something very rare,” Capton said. “Yesterday, when we announced Reese and Hello Sunshine’s arrival at Mediawan, all our producers called us asking: ‘How can we work with them? How can we access the IP? How can we co-produce with them?’ There was a very strong desire from all our producers.”

“The goal isn’t for Reese to produce more herself, because she’s already produced a lot, but for this to also to fuel and create co-productions with our various producers. That’s what we’re hoping for,” he added.

Asked about the skepticism surrounding the Hello Sunshine deal, similar to the doubts raised when Mediawan acquired Plan B, Capton pointed to the latter’s recent hits.

“Plan B has produced ‘F1’ and ‘Adolescence’ last year. They’ve announced a pretty incredible lineup of series and films, so we’re very happy,” Capton said. “We had to trust each other, and it also took time to show what Mediawan was all about.”

Capton also sees further avenues for Mediawan to expand its footprint in the U.S. “We’re going to continue. Peter Chernin ’s arrival at the group has helped us become more ambitious, and with KKR’s support and the help of our local teams, we’re going to do something quite unique.”

While he declined to address rumors that Mediawan was one of the companies circling Lionsgate, he said, “In our model, the more we can distribute worldwide, the better off we’ll be. So, we’re looking at all possible opportunities.”

The French executive, who splits his time between Los Angeles and Paris, is also optimistic about the prospects for groups like Mediawan following the recent Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, even as Skydance prepares to make massive cuts.

“Skydance has committed to producing a certain number of films each year. I believe we have a company built on the creativity of our talent, and so, together, we’ll continue to develop and produce even more,” he said, pointing out that “Backrooms” (North Road), “Adolescence” (Plan B) and Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” (Blue Morning Pictures), starring Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz, were made by producers who are part of Mediawan. He also revealed that the company will soon announce a major deal on vertical formats. “I’m convinced that these successes will only grow with our global consolidation,” Capton concluded.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 1947年出生于纽约的斯蒂芬·肖尔是将彩色摄影作为严肃艺术媒介的摄影师之一。他14岁时，爱德华·斯泰肯就为纽约现代艺术博物馆购买了他的三幅作品，而当他拍摄安迪·沃霍尔工厂的日常生活时，他还是个青少年。1971年，大都会艺术博物馆为他举办了个人展览，使他成为自阿尔弗雷德·斯蒂格利茨以来首位在该馆展出的在世摄影师。次年，他带着一台小型35毫米相机穿越美国，拍摄了《美国表面》（American Surfaces），记录了餐厅、汽车旅馆房间、餐食和陌生人。随后，他改用8×10大画幅相机进行公路旅行，这些旅行最终形成了《非同寻常的地点》（Uncommon Places，1982），成为新彩色摄影运动的里程碑之作。自1982年以来，肖尔一直在巴德学院指导摄影项目，他的著作《摄影的本质》（The Nature of Photographs）仍是全球学生的参考书。

article_text:
Born in New York in 1947, Stephen Shore is one of the photographers who made color a serious medium in American art. He was 14 when Edward Steichen bought three of his prints for the Museum of Modern Art, and still a teenager when he photographed daily life at Andy Warhol’s Factory. In 1971, the Metropolitan Museum of Art gave him a solo show, making him the first living photographer exhibited there since Alfred Stieglitz. The following year, he crossed the United States with a small 35mm camera for “American Surfaces,” a visual diary of diners, motel rooms, meals and strangers. He then switched to an 8×10 view camera for the road trips that became Uncommon Places (1982), a landmark of the New Color generation. Shore has directed the photography program at Bard College since 1982, and his book The Nature of Photographs remains a reference for students worldwide.

On the occasion of his retrospective “Véhiculaire & Vernaculaire,” which was held at the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson in Paris in 2024, Stephen Shore took part in a public conversation with Quentin Bajac, director of the Jeu de Paume, held in the heart of the exhibition. Bajac knows the work closely: as chief curator of photography at the Museum of Modern Art, he organized Shore’s first career-spanning survey in the United States in 2017.

XXI Biennale Città di Penne Stati di Transizione – Transitional States 31 ottobre – 29 novembre 2026 | Penne (PE)

Cinque rassegne, quattro luoghi espositivi principali e un percorso tra arte contemporanea, sperimentazione e nuove possibilità di interpretazione. Dal 31 ottobre al 29 novembre 2026, la XXI Biennale Città di Penne presenta Stati di Transizione – Transitional States , un progetto espositivo articolato in cinque rassegne, distribuite in quattro spazi della Città e dedicate alle ricerche di artisti italiani e internazionali. Promossa dalla Fondazione Musei di Penne, dal Comune di Penne e dall’Accademia di Belle Arti dell’Aquila, con la collaborazione dalla Cooperativa Cogecstre e della Collezione Nato Frascà, la Biennale mette in relazione esperienze artistiche differenti attraverso un tema comune: la transizione, intesa come condizione di passaggio, apertura e trasformazione dei linguaggi. Il progetto assume l’incertezza non come limite, ma come possibilità critica e generativa. Le opere proposte non si esauriscono in dichiarazioni esplicite né ricercano necessariamente esiti formali definitivi: interrogano questioni estetiche, politiche, sociali e percettive, sollecitando il pubblico a costruire interpretazioni, riconoscere contraddizioni e immaginare significati ulteriori. Ne emerge una concezione dell’arte come spazio di ricerca e di confronto, capace di mettere in discussione le convenzioni e di aprire prospettive inedite. Il percorso coinvolge il Museo MaMEC, l’Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, alcuni ambienti dell’ex Tribunale e l’ex Convento del Carmine, intrecciando mostre internazionali, ricerche sui linguaggi contemporanei, approfondimenti storico-artistici e pratiche sperimentali delle nuove generazioni. L’evento di apertura si svolgerà il 31 ottobre alle 16.00 presso la Sala Consiliare, a seguire l’apertura di tutte le sedi espositive, per concludere il pomeriggio con un evento musicale a cura di Fornace del Bono ed Eco Brain, presso la sede dell’ex Convento del Carmine alle ore 20.00. L’orario di apertura delle mostre fino al 29 novembre, sarà il venerdì e il sabato ore 16:00/20:00 • domenica ore 10:00/13:00 16:00/20:00.

• MAMeC Museo d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea, Via Muzio Pansa 37

BRIDGING 2 a cura di Lorand Hegyi

A cura di Lorand Hegyi, Bridging n. 2 prosegue il progetto pluriennale Bridging, nato nell’ambito dell’Aragno Humanities Forum per intensificare la collaborazione tra artisti italiani e internazionali e favorire relazioni dirette tra i protagonisti della cultura. Dopo la prima tappa dedicata a tre artisti italiani appartenenti a una generazione successiva alla Transavanguardia, questa seconda rassegna presenta in Italia le ricerche di Lois Weinberger, Hubert Scheibl e Alois Mosbacher, artisti austriaci accomunati da un approccio capace di mettere in relazione la sperimentazione formale con una più ampia riflessione culturale e sociologica. “Una mostra eccezionale, con artisti internazionali di straordinaria importanza, una proposta inedita in Italia. La prima occasione per la cultura artistica italiana di incontrare la ricerca di tre maestri fondamentali della cultura artista europea”

• Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, Largo San Giovanni Evangelista 121

STATI DI TRANSIZIONE – TRANSITIONAL STATES a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani

La mostra Stati di Transizione – Transitional States, a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani, riunisce artisti che affrontano l’opera d’arte non soltanto attraverso le sue qualità estetiche e stilistiche, ma interrogandone il senso, le modalità di percezione e le possibilità interpretative: arte intesa come spazio di possibilità. In esposizione le opere di Tina Bellini, Francesca Quintilio, Minus Log, Vanessa Di Lodovico, Ugo Giletta, Paolo Chiasera, Alberto Messina, Diego Soldà, Antonio Scaccabarozzi, Luciano Sozio, Marco Cordero, Elena Modorati e Irina Razumovskaya. Le ricerche presentate condividono l’attenzione per linguaggi che si sottraggono alla retorica e alle definizioni rigide. Le forme tradizionali vengono rilette, decostruite e ricomposte; la chiarezza apparente lascia spazio all’insolito, al dubbio, alla contraddizione e alla riduzione all’essenziale.

• Ex Tribunale, Salita Annunziata

La seconda sezione a cura di Sibilla Panerai, Antonio Zimarino, e Franca D’Angelo, presenta una selezione di opere su carta realizzate da Nato Frascà a Parigi tra il 1961 e il 1962, negli anni iniziali della sua ricerca artistica. L’esposizione si inserisce nel ventennale della scomparsa dell’artista, figura centrale della sperimentazione italiana del secondo Novecento e tra i fondatori del Gruppo Uno.

• Ex Convento del Carmine, Via Clemente de Caesaris

QUEL CHE RESTA È MIRAGGIO ACCADEMIA DI BELLE ARTI L’AQUILA a cura di Antonello Antico, Maurizio Coccia e Enzo De Leonibus

Completa il programma della Biennale Quel che resta è miraggio, mostra nata dalla Summer School 2026 dell’Accademia di Belle Arti dell’Aquila, a cura di Antonello Antico, Maurizio Coccia ed Enzo De Leonibus, con coordinamento di Maurizio Coccia e in collaborazione con Gianni Moretti. Svoltasi dal 28 settembre al 4 ottobre La mostra restituisce gli esiti di questo percorso attraverso un insieme eterogeneo di performance, installazioni e opere, espressione delle riflessioni delle nuove generazioni sul tema della transizione e sulle possibilità di sperimentare forme e linguaggi. Gli artisti partecipanti sono Adele Bianchi, Massimo Camplone, Alessandro Crescenzi, Francesco delle Monache, Paolo Di Battista, Valentina Equizi, Gemma Maria La Cecilia, Mattia Pio Mazza, Simone Mostaccioli, Ipek Ansi Ortakol, Giorgia Tatangelo, Alice Tonelli e Denis Tuncbilek.

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is a computer is technology. Technology is useful when you put it in the hands of people, when you put it in the hands of artists who can amplify their voice.

“Technology is not useful when it takes the place of the artist, and that’s the concern with generative AI,” he continued. “It’s an amazing piece of technology, but the concern is that when it supplants the artist, then we have an issue because the computer cannot speak about humanity at all. It doesn’t know what it feels like.”

“Wildwood” is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) who travels into a forbidden forest when her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. It took 16 years to complete the film, Knight said.

“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big sweeping adventure story. It’s a beautiful extravaganza. It’s an epic, but that’s not something that sustains you for 16 years.

He continued, “At the heart of it, it has to be something that means something to you and that’s the thing I’m most proud of is that underneath it all, it is something that is really heartfelt, it’s beautiful, it’s emotional and that’s the thing I hope audiences take away from this.”

But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big… pic.twitter.com/hNeDFa8mCc — Variety (@Variety) October 22, 2026

Knight doesn’t believe that AI could have helped speed up the process — at least not if he wanted to maintain the highest quality. “That very notion fills me with rage,” he said. “Look, that’s the world we live in and the technology seems like it’s only pushing us in one direction, which is everything is going to be simpler. Everything is going to be automated; everything is going to be easier. What I would say to that is that there is something special about the human touch. There is something beautiful about humanity. And that’s one thing that stop motion represents. Stop-motion represents humanity at its finest creativity, emotion, care, devotion, time.

“That’s something that AI could never do because a computer has never felt anything,” Knight added. “It’s never felt loss or love or pain, and that’s something that people can feel and that’s something you feel in something that was made by people.”

The cast of “Wildwood” also includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal.

Bassett talked about recording her work during COVID. “I wanted to get out of the house, get creative again,” she told me. “It was just right on time.”

article_text:
KI kann historische Dokumente täuschend echt verändern – und echte Quellen als Fälschungen erscheinen lassen. Wie ein neues Projekt Archive und Gedenkstätten schützen soll

Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer und Google.org – die gemeinnützige Stiftung des Technologiekonzerns Google – unterstützen gemeinsam ein Projekt gegen die Fälschung von historischen Ausstellungsstücken. Mit der "Global Authentic Memory Initiative" (GAMI) sollen historische Digitalbestände in Archiven, Museen und Gedenkstätten wirksam vor Fälschungen durch generative Künstliche Intelligenz geschützt werden.

Das Bundeskulturministerium stellt für das Projekt Fördermittel in Höhe von 100.000 Euro bereit, weitere 300.000 Euro steuert Google.org bei. GAMI bietet eine herstellerunabhängige und offene technische Lösung an, mit der sich die Echtheit historischer Dokumente digital nachweisen lässt. Dazu werden die Dokumente mit einem digitalen Fingerabdruck mit Verschlüsselungstechnik, einem Zeitstempel sowie einer institutionellen Signatur versehen.

Besuch bei Google

Weimer, der sich in dieser Woche zu Gesprächen mit Vertretern großer US-Technologieunternehmen wie Google und YouTube in den USA aufhielt, betonte die Bedeutung des Projekts: Der Erhalt des kollektiven Gedächtnisses und der Schutz historischer Wahrheiten seien fundamentale Säulen einer wehrhaften Demokratie. Man nehme die Sorgen von Gedenkstätten ernst und schütze wertvolle Archivbestände im digitalen Zeitalter dauerhaft.

Hintergrund der Initiative ist ein Hilferuf von NS-Gedenkstätten in einem offenen Brief vom 13. Januar 2026. Darin warnten die Einrichtungen vor der Gefahr der sogenannten "Lügner-Dividende": Durch den Vormarsch generativer KI bestehe das Risiko, dass echte historische Dokumente fälschlicherweise als KI-Generat abgetan oder synthetische Fälschungen als Tatsachen verbreitet werden. Im Gegensatz zu modernen Medien enthalten historische Objekte meist keine eingebetteten Herkunftsnachweise.

Projekt aus Bayern

GAMI ist ein Projekt des bayerischen Startups Authentic Memory gUG, einer Ausgründung der Technischen Universität München und der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München unter Leitung von Gründer Pablo Toussaint. Erste erfolgreiche Testläufe des Verfahrens gab es bereits mit den KZ-Gedenkstätten Dachau und Flossenbürg.

Ungeachtet der Zusammenarbeit dringt Kulturstaatsminister Weimer weiterhin auf eine regulatorische Verschärfung gegenüber großen Tech-Konzernen: Er plant eine Digitalabgabe für Plattformen wie Google und Meta, um mit den Einnahmen die heimische Medien- und Kulturlandschaft sowie den Lokaljournalismus zu stärken.
